questions.q: At 7 a.m. Asha watches a flower bud in the school garden open and wonders, 'How does it know when to open?' In the chapter's picture of science, what is Asha's wondering?
questions.a: Curiosity, the quality the chapter calls most important for doing science
o: Curiosity, the quality the chapter calls most important for doing science
An experiment, because science is only about doing things with apparatus
A memorised fact, because the chapter says science is about facts and figures
A final answer, because the chapter explains how a flower knows when to bloom

questions.q: Neel has learnt 40 facts about planets by heart but has never wondered about anything he sees. Tara knows fewer facts but keeps asking how her balcony plant knows which way to lean. The student showing what the chapter calls the most important thing for doing science is ___.
questions.a: Tara

questions.q: In a class debate, Vikram argues: 'Science happens in oceans, galaxies and big laboratories. My kitchen and my playground have nothing to do with it.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: Science is everywhere, kitchen and playground included, and discoveries often come from unexpected places
o: Science is everywhere, kitchen and playground included, and discoveries often come from unexpected places
Science is everywhere only after five years of study, so kitchens and playgrounds will count much later on
Kitchens and playgrounds count only if you carry out an experiment with a teacher present in the room
Oceans and galaxies are the real places of science, but a kitchen is allowed as a second-best example

questions.q:
Two students see the same dripping tap. Sunil shrugs: 'Taps drip, so what?' Jaya asks, 'Why does it drip faster at night than in the afternoon?'
(a) Which student is showing curiosity, and what in her words shows it?
(b) Using the chapter, explain why Jaya's question is a better start for science than knowing many facts about taps.
questions.a: (a) Jaya; she notices something and asks why about it. (b) The chapter calls curiosity the most important thing for science, which it describes as a way of thinking, observing and doing; her question starts that process, while a list of facts does not.
s: Part (a): Jaya, because she observes and asks why
Part (b): curiosity is the most important thing, and her question starts thinking, observing and doing

questions.q:
Statement 1: The chapter says science helps us understand the world we live in and uncover the secrets of the universe.
Statement 2: The chapter says that groundbreaking discoveries have come only from well-equipped laboratories.
Statement 3: The chapter asks us to think of science as a big adventure in which we ask questions and explore the world.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 2 only
All three statements

questions.q: Four Grade 6 students are described. Which one is doing what the chapter calls science?
questions.a: Imran sees wet clothes dry at different speeds, asks why, and plans how to find out
o: Imran sees wet clothes dry at different speeds, asks why, and plans how to find out
Joseph learns a list of fifty facts about planets by heart and repeats it to his friends
Kavita copies a neighbour's finished experiment word for word, without wondering about it
Lalit waits for the teacher to say what to observe and never asks anything himself

questions.q: Farhan writes in his notebook: 'Why the stars shine and how a flower knows when to open are two of the mysteries the chapter says science helps us unravel. So science is about rare, faraway wonders, not about ordinary days.' Test Farhan's statement: which part is right and which part is wrong?
questions.a: Partly right. Right: the chapter does give the night sky and a blooming flower as mysteries science helps us unravel. Wrong: a flower opens in an ordinary garden, and the chapter says science is everywhere, from what is cooking in the kitchen to what is happening on the playground, so it is about ordinary days too.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: both are mysteries the chapter says science helps unravel
Wrong part: science is everywhere, including the kitchen and playground, so ordinary days count

questions.q: Differentiate between 'knowing that stars shine' and 'wondering why stars shine', and say which one the chapter treats as the start of science.
questions.a: Knowing is holding a fact; wondering is asking a question about it. The chapter treats the wondering (curiosity, asking how and why) as where science starts.
s: Fact held versus question asked, correctly contrasted
Wondering identified as the start, linked to curiosity

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter calls curiosity the most important thing for doing science.
Reason (R): When we are curious we start posing questions, asking how and why, and that is where finding answers begins.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Plan a 'Science is Everywhere' hunt for Class 4 children with five stops in and around a school. Each stop must be a different place and carry one how or why question for the children to think about; no stop may give the answer. Then explain, using the chapter's description of science, why the hunt counts as science even though it uses no apparatus.
questions.a: E.g. (1) Sandpit: why are some grains of sand darker than others? (2) School kitchen: why does the rice swell when it cooks? (3) Playground: why does a swing slow down by itself? (4) Hill seen from the gate: how did the hill get its shape? (5) Garden: how does a flower know when to open? The stops run from tiny things to massive ones and from everyday places, as the chapter's sand-and-mountains and kitchen-and-playground lines do. It counts as science because science is a way of thinking, observing and doing things to understand the world, and the questions build curiosity, which the chapter calls the most important thing.
s: Five different places, including at least one everyday place such as a kitchen or playground
The places cover both tiny and massive things, as the chapter's sand-to-mountains idea does
Every stop carries a how or why question and gives no answer
Explanation: science is thinking, observing and doing to understand the world
Explanation: the hunt builds curiosity, the most important thing, so apparatus is not what makes it science

questions.q: Rakesh is told, 'Questions like why stars shine or how a flower knows when to open are too hard for Grade 6, so do not ask them.' How does the chapter treat such questions?
questions.a: As mysteries science helps us unravel, so asking them is where it begins
o: As mysteries science helps us unravel, so asking them is where it begins
As questions the chapter answers in its first pages, so asking is unnecessary
As questions for a laboratory only, with no link to everyday curiosity
As questions that should wait until the Grade 6 facts are memorised

questions.q:
Ritika keeps two things on her desk: a pinch of sand in a jar and a photo of a mountain range. She plans to study only the mountain, 'because sand is too small to teach anything'.
(a) Using the chapter's sand-and-mountains idea, say what her plan misses.
(b) Write one how or why question about the sand that she could investigate.
questions.a: (a) The chapter says that whether we study tiny grains of sand or massive mountains, there is always something new and exciting to discover, so the sand is just as worth studying. (b) E.g. Why do some grains of sand sparkle in sunlight while others do not?
s: Part (a): something new to discover at every size, tiny or massive
Part (b): a how or why question about the sand that can be investigated

questions.q:
At Science Week, a school ran two stalls for one day. The Quiz Stall gave visitors a sheet of printed questions with fixed answers; 120 visitors came and none wrote a question of their own. At the Ask-Why Corner, visitors wrote their own how or why questions on sticky notes; 80 visitors came and wrote 56 questions, 30 of them about the sky and stars. Next year there is space for only one stall.
(a) Many quiz sheets were fully correct. Does a fully correct sheet show that the visitor was doing science as the chapter describes it? Give a reason.
(b) A volunteer wants to throw away the 30 sky questions 'because nobody here can answer why stars shine'. What does the chapter say about such questions?
(c) For every 10 visitors, how many questions of their own did each stall collect?
(d) Which stall should run next year? Decide, using your answers above.
questions.a: (a) No; a correct sheet can come from memorised facts, but the chapter describes science as a way of thinking, observing and doing, started by curiosity. (b) The chapter calls questions like why the stars shine mysteries that science helps us unravel, so they should be kept, not thrown away. (c) Ask-Why Corner: 56 per 80 visitors = 7 per 10 visitors; Quiz Stall: 0 per 10. (d) The Ask-Why Corner: although the Quiz Stall drew more visitors (120 against 80), only the Ask-Why Corner made visitors wonder and ask how and why, which is curiosity, the thing the chapter calls most important.
s: No: correct answers can be memorised; science is thinking, observing and doing driven by curiosity
Keep them: the chapter calls such questions mysteries science helps us unravel
7 questions per 10 visitors at the Ask-Why Corner, 0 at the Quiz Stall
The Ask-Why Corner, weighing more quiz visitors against the curiosity the corner produced

questions.q: The chapter calls science a big adventure in which we ask questions, explore and try to understand how things work. Which activity does NOT fit that adventure?
questions.a: Copying a friend's answer on why stars shine without asking anything
o: Copying a friend's answer on why stars shine without asking anything
Exploring a pond near the school to see what lives in and around the water
Asking why the puddles in the yard vanish faster on sunny days
Trying to understand how the brakes of a bicycle stop the wheel

questions.q: Write a short real-life situation (two or three lines) in which a person notices something, asks 'why', and sets out to find out. Say which idea of science from the chapter it shows.
questions.a: E.g. Ishaan sees that the ice cream at the school fair stall melts faster in the open than under the tent. He asks why and moves one cup under the tent to compare. It shows science as thinking, observing and doing, started by curiosity.
s: A noticed event in a real setting
A 'why' question and a step to find out
Linked to science as thinking, observing and doing things, driven by curiosity

questions.q: True or False? A student who has memorised every fact in the Grade 6 science book but never wonders about anything is doing science exactly as the chapter describes it. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter describes science as a way of thinking, observing and doing things, driven by curiosity; memorising facts alone is not that.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: science is thinking, observing and doing, started by curiosity and questions, not facts learnt by heart alone

questions.q:
Four learners are described.
Meera watches ants carry crumbs along the school wall and asks where they are going and why.
Imran can recite 'science is a way of thinking, observing and doing' but has never looked closely at anything.
Pooja sees her tea cool in the cup and says, 'Obviously it cools,' and moves on.
Aman asks 'why' about everything but never tries to find out.
(i) Who observes something closely and then asks why about it? (ii) Who has the words of science but not the habit? (iii) What is Pooja missing? (iv) What is Aman missing, if curiosity is to lead to answers? (v) Meera and Aman both ask why. What does Meera do first that the description of Aman never shows?
questions.a: (i) Meera. (ii) Imran. (iii) Pooja does not wonder; she stops at 'obviously' and does not ask how or why. (iv) Aman asks questions but takes no step to find answers, such as observing or testing. (v) Meera observes something closely (the ants and their crumbs) before asking; the chapter says the first and foremost thing is to be curious and observe your surroundings keenly.
s: Meera: the only one who observes closely and then asks why
Imran identified: words without observing
Pooja: no wondering about what she observes
Aman: questions with no attempt to find out
Meera observes keenly first, which the chapter puts first

questions.q:
A newspaper column claims: 'All great discoveries are made in expensive laboratories, so a child without a laboratory cannot really do science.'
(a) Give a reason from the chapter why the first half of the claim does not hold.
(b) Even if most discoveries did come from laboratories, why would the second half still be wrong? Use a different idea from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The chapter says science is everywhere, from the kitchen to the playground, and that some of the most groundbreaking discoveries have often come from unexpected places, not only laboratories. (b) Doing science does not need a laboratory: anyone who follows the scientific method (observe, ask, guess, test, analyse) is working like a scientist, and the chapter says the most important thing is curiosity.
s: Part (a): science is everywhere and discoveries often come from unexpected places
Part (b): anyone following the method works like a scientist; curiosity matters most

questions.q: The chapter says science runs 'from what is cooking in the kitchen to what is happening on the playground'. Give one question a student could ask in each place, and say what the two questions have in common.
questions.a: E.g. kitchen: why does the dal bubble up when it is cooking? Playground: why does the swing slow down by itself? Both begin with observing and wondering how or why, which is curiosity.
s: One 'why' or 'how' question rooted in a kitchen
One 'why' or 'how' question rooted in a playground
Common feature: both start from observing and curiosity

questions.q:
A class newsletter printed 40 'wonder questions' sent in by students in one month: 16 came from home kitchens, 10 from the school playground, 8 from a TV programme on the ocean depths and 6 from a TV programme on outer space. The newsletter's aim is to show every student that she can do science without travelling or special equipment.
(a) Which line of the chapter is illustrated by questions arriving from all four kinds of place?
(b) One question was 'Why does the pressure cooker whistle?' and another 'Why do stars shine?'. A student says only the second is a real science question. Correct him.
(c) What percentage of the questions came from the kitchen or the playground?
(d) There is room for one feature: 'Questions from far-away places' or 'Questions from your own home and playground'. Which fits the newsletter's aim? Decide, using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) Science is everywhere: from the depths of the ocean to the vastness of outer space, from what is cooking in the kitchen to what is happening on the playground. (b) Both start from noticing something and asking why, which is curiosity; the kitchen is one of the places the chapter names, and discoveries often come from unexpected places. (c) 26 of 40 = 65%. (d) 'Questions from your own home and playground': it holds 26 questions (65%) against 14, and it shows that the curiosity science needs is possible without travel or equipment, which is the newsletter's aim.
s: Science is everywhere, ocean depths to outer space, kitchen to playground
Both are science: both start from curiosity, and the kitchen is a place the chapter names
Home and playground feature, justified with 26 against 14 and the aim

questions.q: A research team finds new evidence showing that an explanation accepted earlier was wrong. In the chapter's jigsaw picture of science, what does this correspond to?
questions.a: A wrongly placed piece is moved and our understanding changes
o: A wrongly placed piece is moved and our understanding changes
A piece is thrown away and the puzzle is declared finished for good
A piece is added without any other piece or idea being affected
The puzzle has reached its limit and nothing more can be found

questions.q:
A class 'Facts Board' had 16 cards at the start of term. During the term the class pinned up 6 new cards, and found that 3 of the old cards had been placed in the wrong column, so it shifted them to the right one.
(a) How many cards are on the board at the end of term?
(b) In the chapter's jigsaw comparison, which changes were 'adding pieces' and which were 'moving pieces'?
questions.a: (a) 16 + 6 = 22 cards; shifting 3 cards does not change the count. (b) The 6 new cards are pieces added by new discoveries; the 3 shifted cards are pieces that were in the wrong place and were moved.
s: Part (a): 22 cards, since moved cards are not extra cards
Part (b): 6 new cards are added pieces, 3 shifted cards are moved pieces

questions.q: Nikhil grumbles, 'Why should I care about adding pieces to the science puzzle? That is only for scientists.' Which point from the chapter answers him best?
questions.a: Some of what we find out is useful in our daily lives
o: Some of what we find out is useful in our daily lives
Every piece, once placed, stays fixed in its place for ever
The puzzle is already complete for Grade 6 students
Only trained scientists are allowed to add new pieces

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter calls science a giant and unending jigsaw puzzle.
Reason (R): Every discovery removes a question from the puzzle, so the number of open questions keeps falling.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A shop sells a 500-piece jigsaw with the finished picture printed on its box. Give two ways in which the chapter's science puzzle is different from it.
questions.a: (1) The shop puzzle ends when the 500th piece is placed, but the science puzzle has no limit, because every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions. (2) In the shop puzzle a correctly fitted piece stays put, but in science a piece is sometimes found in the wrong place and has to be moved as new discoveries change our understanding.
s: No limit: each new piece leads to more questions, unlike a fixed 500 pieces
Pieces can be found in the wrong place and moved, unlike a fixed picture

questions.q:
Match each situation (1-4) with the jigsaw idea (A-D) it fits.
1. A town's earlier belief is revised after a better test
2. A researcher reports an observation never made before
3. After solving one problem, a class has five new questions
4. A teacher says that however long people work, new things will remain to be found out
A. A new piece is added
B. A piece is moved because it was in the wrong place
C. Each piece leads to more questions
D. There is no limit to what we can discover

Jatin argues: 'There is no limit to what science can discover. So there is no point in discovering anything, because we will never finish.' Evaluate his argument: what is right in it and what is wrong?
questions.a: Partly right. Right: the chapter does say there is no limit to what we can discover. Wrong: the chapter calls this the best thing about the puzzle, not a reason to stop; every discovery adds a piece, and some of what we find out is useful in our daily lives, so discovering is worthwhile even though the puzzle never ends.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: there is no limit to what we can discover
Wrong part: no limit is the best thing about the puzzle, and each piece adds knowledge useful in daily life

questions.q: Over a term, Class 6 finds that what it learnt about water while studying weather also helps explain something about cooking food. Which idea from the chapter's jigsaw passage does this fit?
questions.a: As we discover more, we realise that ideas are all connected
o: As we discover more, we realise that ideas are all connected
A piece was in the wrong place, so it must be thrown out
The puzzle has a limit, and the class has now reached it
Each piece stands alone and has nothing at all to do with the others

questions.q:
A class starts a term with 5 unanswered questions. Each week it answers 3 questions, and each answered question raises 2 new ones.
(i) How many questions are unanswered at the end of week 1?
(ii) Continue the count to the end of week 5.
(iii) How many weeks of answering would it take to reach zero if this pattern continues?
(iv) Which sentence of the chapter does this pattern mirror?
(v) The class worries that it is 'falling behind'. Using the chapter, explain why a growing list is not a failure.
questions.a: (i) 5 - 3 + 6 = 8. (ii) 8, 11, 14, 17, 20. (iii) It never reaches zero, since the list rises by 3 a week. (iv) Every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions and more things to find out. (v) The chapter calls the fact that there is no limit to what we can discover the best thing about the puzzle; more questions means more knowledge has been gained, not lost.
s: Net rise of 3 a week, so never zero
Chapter sentence: every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions
Growing list explained as the no-limit puzzle, not a failure

questions.q:
A poster shows a jigsaw puzzle. Six pieces fit together in the middle. A seventh piece sits outside the picture with a curved arrow from an old gap to a new gap, labelled 'moved'. Along the right edge are three empty dotted outlines, each with a '?' inside, and the edge itself has no border line.
(a) What does the piece with the 'moved' arrow stand for in the chapter's comparison?
(b) What do the dotted outlines and the missing border stand for?
questions.a: (a) A piece that had been put in the wrong place and was moved, because a new discovery changed our understanding. (b) The new questions that each piece of knowledge leads to, and the fact that the puzzle has no limit (no edge where it ends).
s: Part (a): a wrongly placed piece moved as understanding changes
Part (b): more questions to find out, and no limit to the puzzle

questions.q: Dhruv's group records 4 observations, and each raises 3 new questions, so the group ends the week with 12 new questions. What does this tell the group about its 'puzzle', in the chapter's terms?
questions.a: It is growing, as each piece brings more to find out
o: It is growing, as each piece brings more to find out
It is nearly finished, as 4 questions are now answered
It has shrunk to 8 pieces, as 12 minus 4 makes 8
It has a limit of 12, after which nothing will be left

questions.q: True or False? A class that learns how soil holds water, and then sees that this explains why plants in one corner of its garden grow better, is seeing what the chapter describes as ideas being connected. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says that as we discover more and more, we start realising that ideas are all connected; here one piece of knowledge (about soil) explains another observation (about plants).
s: Verdict: True
Reason: as we discover more we realise ideas are connected, and the soil idea explains the plant observation

questions.q:
The science club's Puzzle Wall has one card per discovery made by the club. In Term 1 it posted 18 cards; later, better tests showed 5 of them were wrong, and they were shifted to a 'changed understanding' column with a note on what replaced them. In Term 2 it posted 24 new cards and shifted 6. The principal wants the shifted cards taken down to keep the wall neat.
(a) In which term was a larger share of the posted cards shifted? Show the percentages.
(b) One shifted card had sat in the 'answered' column for a whole term. In the chapter's comparison, what does its move stand for, and does it make the Term 1 work useless?
(c) Should the club agree to take the shifted cards down? Decide, using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Term 1: 5/18 = 27.8%; Term 2: 6/24 = 25%. Term 1 had the larger share. (b) It is a piece that had been put in the wrong place and was moved because a new discovery changed understanding; the Term 1 work is not useless, since the move is how understanding grows. (c) No; keep them, labelled. About a quarter of each term's cards were shifted (11 of 42 in all), and the chapter treats moving wrongly placed pieces as a normal part of science, so taking them down would hide how the club's understanding changed. Neatness can be kept by giving the column a clear heading.
s: 27.8% against 25%, so Term 1
A wrongly placed piece moved as understanding changes, not wasted work
Keep the shifted cards: moving pieces is normal in the chapter's puzzle, and they show a quarter of the wall's story (11 of 42)

questions.q:
Statement 1: In the chapter's puzzle, every piece stays exactly where it was first placed.
Statement 2: The chapter says some of what we will find out is useful in our daily lives.
Statement 3: The chapter says that as we discover more, ideas turn out to be separate and unconnected.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q: Suppose each answered question raises at least one new question. Show that science cannot reach a point where every question has been answered.
questions.a: Start with any list of questions. Answering one removes it but adds at least one new question, so after any number of answers at least one question remains. The list never reaches zero, which matches the chapter's puzzle with no limit.
s: State the assumption: each answer raises at least one new question
Show that the count never falls to zero after any answer
Link to the chapter: the puzzle has no limit

questions.q:
A letter to a newspaper complains: 'Science books changed their explanation, so science cannot be trusted.'
(a) Which idea from the chapter explains why explanations can change?
(b) Use it to write a one-line reply to the letter.
questions.a: (a) A piece of the puzzle may have been put in the wrong place and need to be moved; new discoveries often change our understanding. (b) A changed explanation shows the puzzle is being put together better as new discoveries come in, not that science is useless.
s: Part (a): wrongly placed piece moved; new discoveries change understanding
Part (b): a reply that change is part of growing knowledge

questions.q: Which statement does NOT fit the chapter's jigsaw comparison?
questions.a: The puzzle will be finished once its last piece is placed
o: The puzzle will be finished once its last piece is placed
Every new discovery adds another piece to the puzzle
New discoveries often change our understanding of the world
As we discover more, we realise the ideas are connected

questions.q: Differentiate between a discovery that 'adds a piece' and one that 'moves a piece' in the jigsaw comparison.
questions.a: Adding a piece puts new knowledge into the puzzle; moving a piece corrects an earlier placement, so our understanding of something already known changes.
s: Adding: new knowledge added
Moving: an earlier idea corrected, understanding changes

questions.q: Write a short situation from school life in which finding the answer to one question leads to at least two new questions. Then name the chapter's idea it shows.
questions.a: E.g. Leena finds that the classroom plant drooped because it was not watered over the holiday. That raises new questions: how many days can it go without water, and why does the plant by the window droop sooner? It shows that every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions and more things to find out.
s: One question answered in a realistic school setting
At least two new questions that follow from that answer
Chapter idea: every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions

questions.q: A 'quiz book' has 200 questions, each with a fixed answer printed at the back. Compare it with science as the chapter's jigsaw describes it. Give four differences, then judge which one better prepares a student for a question nobody has asked before.
questions.a: (1) The quiz book has a fixed set of 200 questions; in the puzzle every discovery adds a new piece. (2) A printed answer never changes; a wrongly placed piece of the puzzle can be moved as new discoveries change our understanding. (3) The quiz book ends at question 200; the puzzle has no limit. (4) Answering a quiz question closes it; each new piece of the puzzle leads to more questions. Judgement: the puzzle picture prepares a student better, because it trains her to keep asking and to revise what she thinks, which is what a new question needs.
s: Difference: a fixed set versus pieces added by each discovery
Difference: unchanging answers versus wrongly placed pieces moved
Difference: a last question versus no limit
Difference: answers close questions versus new pieces leading to more questions
Judgement for the puzzle picture, with a reason

questions.q:
A class recorded 30 answers in a month. Later, 4 of these answers were changed after new observations, and the class also logged 45 new questions that the answers had raised. The teacher has Rs 1,500 to buy one notebook each for 40 students. Notebook A (one column: answers) costs Rs 25. Notebook B (three columns: answers, changed answers, new questions) costs Rs 35.
(a) In Notebook B, which column would show the chapter's idea that every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions, and which would show that a piece of the puzzle can be put in the wrong place?
(b) On average, how many new questions came from each recorded answer, and what does a value above 1 show about the limit of the puzzle?
(c) Of the month's 79 records (answers, changes and new questions), what percentage would Notebook A have no place for?
(d) Which notebook should the teacher buy for all 40 students? Decide, using the costs and (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) The new-questions column shows that each new piece leads to more questions; the changed-answers column shows pieces that were wrongly placed and had to be moved. (b) 45/30 = 1.5; each answer raised more than one new question, so the puzzle keeps growing and there is no limit to what can be discovered. (c) Notebook A has no place for the 4 changes and 45 new questions: 49/79 = 62.0%. (d) Notebook B: 40 x Rs 35 = Rs 1,400, within the Rs 1,500 budget. A costs Rs 1,000 and saves Rs 400, but it has no place for 62% of the records, which are the changed pieces and new questions the chapter says are how knowledge grows.
s: New-questions column for more questions; changed-answers column for wrongly placed pieces
45/30 = 1.5, so the puzzle has no limit
Notebook B: Rs 1,400 is within budget, and A would lose the changes and new questions

questions.q:
Statement 1: The preview uses everyday objects such as a paper sheet, a metal key and a plastic ruler to ask how plants and animals grow.
Statement 2: The preview asks how plants and animals grow, after mentioning a seed and a caterpillar.
Statement 3: The preview says that along with food, we need water to survive.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Priya's grandmother's spice tin tipped over, and mustard seeds got mixed with salt. Priya wonders how the two could be got apart again. Which question from the chapter's preview is she asking?
questions.a: How do we separate different materials from one another?
o: How do we separate different materials from one another?
What are the many dishes of India's different cuisines made of?
How do these plants and animals grow in their regions?
How do we understand hot and cold in water and bodies?

questions.q:
A bag holds a paper cup, a metal key and a rubber eraser.
(a) Write one 'what is it made of' question the chapter's preview would encourage.
(b) Write one 'how do we separate' question the preview would encourage.
questions.a: (a) E.g. Are the key and the eraser made of different materials? (b) E.g. How could we separate the key from the eraser and the paper if they were mixed together?
s: Part (a): a 'made of' question about the objects
Part (b): a 'separate' question about the mixed objects

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter's preview says that water boils and becomes steam when it is heated.
Reason (R): The preview also says that water freezes and becomes ice when it is cooled.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Rohit writes in his notebook, 'The chapter proves that no other planet in the universe has life.' Which correction is accurate to the chapter?
questions.a: Earth is the only planet we know that supports life
o: Earth is the only planet we know that supports life

questions.q:
A class put 20 questions in a box: 5 on life on Earth, 3 on food, 4 on materials, 6 on water and hot and cold, and 2 on space beyond Earth.
(i) Which topic has the most questions, and what percentage is it?
(ii) What percentage are on food and materials together?
(iii) The teacher adds 5 more questions, all on space beyond Earth. What percentage of the new total is now on space?
(iv) After the addition, does water and hot and cold still hold the largest share? Show the percentages.
(v) Which line of the preview invites the class to ask about space at all, even though the book starts with our home, planet Earth?
questions.a: (i) Water and hot and cold: 6/20 = 30%. (ii) (3 + 4)/20 = 35%. (iii) (2 + 5)/25 = 28%. (iv) No: space is now 7/25 = 28% and water and hot and cold is 6/25 = 24%, so space holds the largest share.
