questions.q: Differentiate between 'Earth supports life' and 'Earth is the only planet we know that supports life'. Why does the second wording matter?
questions.a: The first says only that life is found on Earth. The second adds that, as far as we know, no other planet has been found to support life; it does not claim that none exists. The wording keeps the claim within what is known.
s: First statement correctly described
Second adds 'we know', so it claims no more than what is known

questions.q: Aman's sister has a fever and he wonders how anyone can tell how hot she is. Which part of the preview does this question belong with?
questions.a: Hot and cold: finding out how hot something is can matter
o: Hot and cold: finding out how hot something is can matter
The Sun, the Moon and the millions of stars in the sky
The paper, key, ruler and eraser kept in a school box
A caterpillar changing into a butterfly, as an example of growth

questions.q: Imran's revision notes say: 'Chapter 1 explains why water freezes and why it boils.' Is his note accurate? Give your verdict and support it from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The preview only says that water freezes when cooled and boils when heated, and asks questions such as why and how it rains and how we understand hot and cold. It gives no explanations; its job is to spark questions that later chapters take up.
s: Verdict: no
The chapter only states and asks about freezing, boiling and rain
No explanation is given; the preview sparks questions

questions.q:
At a school exhibition, five zones followed the chapter's preview: Earth and life, food, materials, water and hot and cold, and beyond Earth. Visitors posted question slips in the zone they were visiting: Earth and life 64, food 48, materials 36, water and hot and cold 52, beyond Earth 20 (220 slips). Volunteers then found 11 slips in the food zone that asked what a steel plate or a plastic lunch box is made of.
(a) To which zone do the 11 slips belong, according to the preview?
(b) Why might visitors have posted them in the food zone, and which preview question shows where they really belong?
(c) After moving the 11 slips, what percentage of the 220 slips is in the materials zone?
(d) Next year only four zones can run, so two must merge: food with Earth and life, or materials with water and hot and cold. Which merger does the preview itself support? Decide, using the counts after the move.
questions.a: (a) Materials. (b) A plate and a lunch box hold food, so the food zone looked right; but the preview asks of everyday things, such as the cup we drink milk in, 'What are they made of? Are they made of different materials?', which puts them under materials. (c) 36 + 11 = 47; 47/220 = 21.4%. (d) Food with Earth and life: the preview links them directly ('to grow, we need food to eat'), while it gives no link between materials and water. The merged zone would hold 64 + 37 = 101 slips against 47 + 52 = 99 for the other pair, so the numbers are almost equal and the preview's own link decides it.
s: Materials
They hold food, but the preview's 'what are they made of?' question belongs to materials
Food with Earth and life, because the preview links growth and food (101 against 99 slips)

questions.q:
Two classmates, one from Kerala and one from Punjab, open very different lunch boxes.
(a) Which feature of India does the preview connect with this difference?
(b) Write two questions of your own about your friend's lunch: one of the kind the preview asks about what dishes are made of, and one about how we would find out.
questions.a: (a) India is a large and diverse country with different cuisines and many tasty dishes. (b) E.g. 'What is this avial made of?' and 'How could we find out which vegetables are in it?'; the first matches 'What are they made of?', the second 'How do we find out?'.
s: Part (a): a large, diverse country with different cuisines
Part (b): one made-of question and one how-do-we-find-out question about the dish

questions.q: A teacher sorts the class's questions under the chapter's preview topics. Which sorting is wrong?
questions.a: 'Why does water turn into ice?' placed under materials around us
o: 'Why does water turn into ice?' placed under materials around us
'How does a seed grow into a plant?' placed under life on Earth
'Is a key made of a different material from a ruler?' under materials
'What lies beyond Earth, among the Sun and the stars?' under space

questions.q: The topic is growth in living things. Write one question in the style of the chapter's preview, name the example from the chapter it builds on, and say what makes it a good question to investigate.
questions.a: E.g. How does a seed grow into a plant over the days after it is sown? It builds on the chapter's seed growing into a plant; it is investigable because it can be observed day by day.
s: A question about growth
Built on one of the chapter's examples (seed or caterpillar)
A reason it can be investigated

questions.q:
Each student statement (1-4) misreads the chapter's preview. Match it with what it misses (A-D).
1. 'A seed growing into a plant has nothing to do with food.'
2. 'A plastic ruler and a rubber eraser raise no questions; they are just things in a box.'
3. 'Food is the same all over India.'
4. 'Water is only for drinking, so there is nothing to ask about it.'
A. To grow, we need food to eat
B. What are they made of? Are they made of different materials?
C. Across the country we have different cuisines
D. Questions on rain, freezing, boiling and how hot it is

True or False? In the preview, the question 'Why and how does it rain?' is placed with water, not with the Sun, the Moon and the stars, even though rain falls from the sky. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The preview asks about rain in its paragraph on water (after jumping in a puddle when it rained), and keeps the Sun, the Moon and the stars for its later step beyond Earth.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: rain is asked about with water; the Sun, Moon and stars come in the beyond-Earth part

questions.q:
Place each new question under one of the preview's five topics (life on Earth; food; materials; water and hot and cold; beyond Earth), and give a reason from the preview for each. Watch out: some look as if they belong elsewhere.
(i) How does a nurse find out how hot a patient with fever is?
(ii) Why do some birds live only near the sea and others only in deserts?
(iii) What is the dish idli made of, and how could we find out?
(iv) How could iron pins mixed with sawdust be separated?
(v) Why does the Moon look different on different nights?
questions.a: (i) Water and hot and cold, not life: the preview says that whether it is water or our own body when we have fever, finding out how hot something is can be important. (ii) Life on Earth: the preview speaks of the variety of plants and animals that survive and thrive in different regions. (iii) Food: the preview asks of India's dishes 'What are they made of? How do we find out?'. (iv) Materials: the preview asks how we separate different materials from one another. (v) Beyond Earth: the preview says not to limit our questions to Earth and names the Moon.
s: (i) Water and hot and cold, because the preview puts a body with fever with finding out how hot something is
(ii) Life on Earth: variety of life thriving in different regions
(iii) Food: what dishes are made of and how we find out
(iv) Materials: separating materials from one another
(v) Beyond Earth: the Moon, with no need to limit questions to Earth

questions.q: A teacher holds up a leaf, rolls a toy car across the desk and peels a peanut, saying the coming chapters will make students ask questions about all three. Which hope of the book, stated after the preview, is she pointing to?
questions.a: That each chapter will ignite the students' spirit of inquiry
o: That each chapter will ignite the students' spirit of inquiry
That each chapter will give final answers to every question
That each chapter will deal with life on Earth and nothing else
That each chapter can be finished without asking any questions

questions.q:
Divya's question list reads: (1) How does a seed grow? (2) What is a ruler made of? (3) Why do the stars shine? Her friend says (3) does not belong, because the preview 'starts off by looking at our home, planet Earth'.
(a) Is the friend right? Give a reason.
(b) Divya wants to add 'Why does the Moon look different on different nights?' and 'How does a caterpillar become a butterfly?'. Her friend says the first must go too. Judge each question against the preview, with a reason.
(c) Write one more question of the same kind as (3).
questions.a: (a) No; starting with Earth does not mean stopping there: the preview goes on to say we need not limit our questions to the Earth alone. (b) Both belong. The Moon question fits the preview's step beyond Earth, where it names the Sun, the Moon and the stars; the caterpillar question fits life on Earth, where it mentions a caterpillar turning into a butterfly. (c) E.g. Why does the Sun look bigger at sunrise than at noon?
s: Part (a): the friend is wrong; the preview starts with Earth but does not stop there
Part (b): Moon question belongs beyond Earth, caterpillar question under life on Earth
Part (c): a question about the Sun, the Moon or the stars

questions.q: A classmate says that growth in living things only means becoming taller. Using the chapter's two examples, explain why this is incomplete.
questions.a: The chapter mentions a seed growing into a plant and a caterpillar transforming into a butterfly. The caterpillar becoming a butterfly is a change of form, not just height.
s: The two examples named
Caterpillar to butterfly shows a change of form, so growth is more than height

questions.q:
A school near a lake keeps a bird record. In 2019 its eco-club counted 14 different kinds of birds at the lake. In 2024, after part of the lake was filled in for a parking lot, it counted 9 kinds. The school now wants to fill in another part of the lake to build a playground, which the students also want.
(a) By what percentage did the number of kinds of birds fall?
(b) Which idea in the preview about living things on Earth does the 2019 count of 14 kinds illustrate?
(c) Which line of the preview about Earth does the eco-club's worry reflect?
(d) Should the school fill in more of the lake for the playground? Decide, using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) (14 - 9)/14 = 35.7%. (b) The amazing variety of life on Earth: plants and animals that survive and thrive in different regions. (c) Earth has an environment that we must protect. (d) No. The lake is a region where a variety of birds thrive, the record already shows a fall of about 36% after the last filling, and the preview says Earth's environment is one we must protect; the playground, though wanted, should be built somewhere that does not shrink the lake.
s: Variety of life surviving and thriving in different regions
Earth has an environment we must protect
No: the 35.7% fall and the duty to protect the environment outweigh the playground

questions.q: Mohan's notes on a bicycle bell that will not ring got jumbled. P: Maybe the spring inside is rusty. Q: The bell does not ring when I press it. R: So the rusty spring was the reason. S: Why does it not ring? T: I oiled the spring and pressed the bell; it rang. Which order follows the chapter's steps?
questions.a: Q, S, P, T, R
o: Q, S, P, T, R
S, Q, P, T, R
Q, P, S, T, R
Q, S, P, R, T

questions.q:
Ravi's pen stops writing.
(a) Write the first guess the chapter makes and the test that checks it.
(b) The refill turns out to be empty. What does Ravi now know, and which step of the method is he carrying out when he decides this?
questions.a: (a) Guess: the ink has finished. Test: open the pen and check the ink refill. (b) He knows his guess was correct; deciding this from what he saw is analysing the result to see if it answers his question.
s: Part (a): guess that the ink finished, tested by opening the pen and checking the refill
Part (b): the guess was correct, which is the analysis step

questions.q: Sana sees her balcony plant drooping, wonders why, and says, 'Maybe I forgot to water it yesterday.' In the chapter's steps, what is 'maybe I forgot to water it'?
questions.a: A guess, a possible answer to her question
o: A guess, a possible answer to her question
An observation of something she does not understand
A test carried out through an experiment
An analysis of the results of a test

questions.q: Ramesh's torch does not light. He wonders why, guesses that the cells are used up, puts in new cells, and sees the torch light. He has observed, asked, guessed and tested; the step of the chapter's method still left before he can say the cells were the cause is the ___ of the results.
questions.a: analysis

questions.q: A tap in the school corridor drips. Four notes are made: the tap drips; why does it drip?; maybe the washer is worn; the washer is replaced and the tap is watched for an hour. Which note is the test?
questions.a: The washer is replaced and the tap watched for an hour
o: The washer is replaced and the tap watched for an hour
The tap in the school corridor is noticed to be dripping
The question 'why does it drip?' is written in the book
The guess that the washer is worn out is written down

questions.q: Hari guessed that his refill was empty and checked by holding the refill up to the light and looking closely. His friend Ayaan says that was not a real test because Hari did no experiment. Hari claims it was a proper test. Is Hari's claim correct? Give your verdict and the reason from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, Hari is right. The chapter says we test a guess through experiments or more observations; looking closely at the refill is a further observation that can show whether the guess is right, just as in the chapter's pen example, where the refill is checked by opening the pen.
s: Verdict: yes, Hari's claim is correct
The chapter allows a test through experiments or more observations
Looking at the refill checks the guess, as in the pen example

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the chapter's method, we think of a question before we observe anything.
Reason (R): The chapter's first step is to observe something that we find interesting or do not understand.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: Differentiate between a 'guess' and a 'test' in the pen example.
questions.a: A guess is a possible answer to the question (the ink has finished); a test is the check of that guess (opening the pen and looking at the refill).
s: Guess: a possible answer
Test: checking the guess by experiment or observation, with the pen example

questions.q: The window of your classroom will not close. Write five lines, one for each step of the chapter's method, that show how you would investigate. Mention what you would observe, the question, a guess, a test and how you would analyse the result.
questions.a: Observe: the window stops before closing. Question: why will it not close? Guess: something is stuck in the track. Test: look along the track and remove anything found, then try again. Analyse: if it closes, the guess is supported; if not, make a new guess.
s: Observation
Question
Guess
Test
Analysis of the result with the next step

questions.q: Kiran notices that her pen writes on paper but leaves no mark on the glossy cover of her notebook, and she cannot see why. In the chapter's steps, what is 'it leaves no mark on the glossy cover'?
questions.a: An observation of something she does not understand
o: An observation of something she does not understand
A guess at a possible answer to the question in her mind
A test carried out through an experiment
An analysis of what the results of a test show

questions.q:
A poster in the corridor says: 'Science = memorising facts + doing experiments.'
(a) What does the chapter say science is about, beyond these two?
(b) Use the pen example to show that no memorised fact was needed to find the answer.
questions.a: (a) Following a step-by-step process that helps us find answers to our questions. (b) In the pen example the person simply asks why the pen stopped, guesses the ink finished, opens the pen to check the refill, and makes another guess if needed; every step uses observing and testing, not a fact learnt by heart.
s: Part (a): a step-by-step process that helps us find answers
Part (b): the pen answer came from asking, guessing and checking, not from a memorised fact

questions.q:
Thirty students in Class 6B reported pens that stopped writing. They guessed the ink had finished, and 18 refills were found empty. For the other 12, they made a second guess, that the ink had dried, and 5 of those pens wrote again after the tip was rubbed on rough paper. The other 7 are still unexplained.
(a) When 12 refills turned out not to be empty, the class did not stop. What did it do next, and is that what the chapter says to do?
(b) One student says the 18 empty refills prove that 'ink running out' is why every pen stops. Which step of the method is she doing wrongly, and how?
(c) What percentage of the 30 pens has either guess explained so far, and what percentage is still unexplained?
(d) There is time for one more test on the 7 pens: (P) rub each tip on rough paper again, for longer, or (Q) put each refill into a pen body that is known to work. Which test should the class choose? Decide, using the results.
questions.a: (a) It made another guess (the ink had dried) and tried something else to test it; yes, this is exactly what the chapter does when the refill is found not empty. (b) Analysis: the results answer the question only for those 18 pens; 12 refills were not empty, so 'ink running out' cannot explain every pen. (c) (18 + 5)/30 = 23/30 = 76.7% explained; 7/30 = 23.3% still unexplained. (d) Test Q. Test P repeats the dried-ink guess, which has already been tested on these 7 pens and failed; Q tests a new guess, whether the fault is in the refill or in the pen body, so whatever happens it gives new information.
s: A second guess made and tested, as the chapter does when the ink is not finished
Analysis done wrongly: 12 refills were not empty, so the result does not cover every pen
23/30 = 76.7% explained, 7/30 = 23.3% unexplained
Test Q, because P repeats a guess already tested and Q tests a new one

questions.q: Tanu's first guess about her stopped pen turns out to be wrong. Arjun says, 'So the scientific method has failed.' How does the chapter's pen example answer him?
questions.a: A wrong guess is not a failure: another guess is made and tested
o: A wrong guess is not a failure: another guess is made and tested
He is right, because a good guess is always correct the first time
He is right, because after one wrong test the question is dropped
A wrong guess shows that the pen example does not use the method

questions.q: Show that the guess 'the ink has finished' cannot be accepted as the answer before it is tested.
questions.a: A guess is only a possible answer. If the refill is opened and found to have ink, the guess is wrong; only a test can show which. So without a test we do not know whether the guess is right.
s: A guess is only a possible answer
A test can show it wrong (refill with ink)
Therefore it cannot be accepted untested

questions.q: True or False? If a test shows that a guess is wrong, the scientific method has failed and the question should be dropped. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. In the pen example a wrong guess leads to another guess, which is tested in turn.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the method continues with another guess and another test

questions.q:
Statement 1: A guess can be tested through experiments or through more observations.
Statement 2: After a test, we analyse the results to see whether they answer our question.
Statement 3: In the chapter's list of steps, observing comes before thinking of a question.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q: A pen investigation ended with the result 'the refill still had ink'. Write the question, the guess and the test that could have led to this result.
questions.a: Question: why did my pen stop writing? Guess: the ink has finished. Test: open the pen and look at the refill, which was found to still have ink.
s: Question
Guess
Test that gives that result

questions.q: Give an example of a test that is only 'more observations' and uses no apparatus, and say which guess it would test.
questions.a: E.g. holding the pen's refill up against the light and looking for ink inside tests the guess that the ink has finished.
s: A test that is observation only
The guess it tests

questions.q: Which action is NOT a step of the chapter's scientific method?
questions.a: Accepting a guess as true without testing it
o: Accepting a guess as true without testing it
Wondering and thinking of a question
Testing a guess through experiments or more observations
Analysing the results to see if they answer the question

questions.q:
Four students wrote about a stopped pen.
A: The pen stopped. I think the ink is finished. So the pen is bad.
B: The pen stopped. I opened it and the refill was empty.
C: The pen stopped. Why? Maybe the ink dried. I tried it on rough paper and it wrote again. So the ink had dried.
D: Why did my pen stop? Maybe ink finished. Maybe ink dried. Maybe the cap is loose.
(i) A reaches a conclusion. Which step, put in before it, would show whether A's guess is right? (ii) B opens the pen at once. Which two steps does B skip between noticing and opening it? (iii) D lists three guesses. What must D do before it can choose between them? (iv) Which write-up follows the steps best? (v) What should A do next?
questions.a: (i) A test, such as opening the pen and checking the refill. (ii) B does not state a question or a guess before testing. (iii) Test the guesses, one at a time, as the chapter does with the finished and then the dried ink. (iv) C. (v) Open the pen and look at the refill, then analyse the result.
s: A: a test before the conclusion
B: question and guess skipped
D: must test the guesses one by one
C chosen as the best
A's next step: test, then analyse

questions.q:
A school water bottle drips at the cap, 12 drops a minute. Guess 1: the cap is loose. After the cap is tightened, it drips 9 drops a minute. Guess 2: the rubber ring is worn. After the ring is replaced, the bottle is watched for 5 minutes with no drips. A new bottle costs Rs 180; a rubber ring costs Rs 30.
(a) By what percentage did tightening the cap reduce the dripping?
(b) Was guess 1 fully or only partly supported? Why?
(c) Which step of the chapter's method is it when the class compares 12, 9 and 0 drops?
(d) The class can either buy a new bottle now, or first watch the repaired bottle for a whole school day and decide after. Which does the chapter's method support? Decide.
questions.a: (a) (12 - 9)/12 = 25%. (b) Partly: the drips fell but did not stop. (c) Analysing the results. (d) Watch it for a whole day first. Five minutes is a short test, and the chapter says we test a guess through experiments or more observations and then analyse the results; if the bottle stays dry, the Rs 30 repair saves Rs 150 on a new bottle, and if it drips again, a new guess can be made.
s: Partly supported: reduced but not stopped
Analysis of the results
Watch longer first: more observations before deciding, with the Rs 150 saving

questions.q: Rani's dal spills out of the cooker. She wonders whether she put in too much water and uses less next time to see what happens. Which pair is correct?
questions.a: Her guess is 'too much water' and using less water is the test
o: Her guess is 'too much water' and using less water is the test
Her guess is 'less water' and the spilled dal is the test
Her observation is 'too much water'; her guess is 'spilled dal'
She is not following the method, because cooking is not science

questions.q:
Match each moment (1-4) from the chapter's everyday 'scientists' with the step of the method it shows (A-D).
1. The cook uses less water the next day and watches the cooker
2. The electrician notices the bulb stays dark when the switch is on
3. The repair person thinks, 'Maybe a thorn made a hole near the valve'
4. The cook sees no spill with less water and decides too much water was the cause
A. Observing
B. Guessing a possible answer
C. Testing a guess
D. Analysing the results

An electrician's classroom bulb does not light, and she asks whether the problem is with the bulb or the switch.
(a) She moves the bulb to a holder whose switch is known to work, and it lights. Which of her two possible causes does this rule out?
(b) Which cause should she test next, and which step is she doing when she decides the fault from that test?
questions.a: (a) It rules out the bulb, because the bulb works in another holder. (b) The switch; deciding the fault from the result is analysing the results.
s: Part (a): the bulb is ruled out because it lights elsewhere
Part (b): test the switch next; deciding from the result is analysis

questions.q: A bicycle repair person sees a flat tyre and asks, 'From where did the air leak out?' What does the chapter say about her at that moment?
questions.a: She is working like a scientist, as she asks a question to find the cause
o: She is working like a scientist, as she asks a question to find the cause
She is not a scientist, because she works in a repair shop and not a laboratory
She is a scientist only after she has written a report on the tyre
She is memorising facts about tyres, which is all that science needs

questions.q:
Over five days, Rani used different amounts of water for the same amount of dal. Monday: 3 cups, no spill. Tuesday: 4 cups, spill. Wednesday: 3.5 cups, no spill. Thursday: 4 cups, spill. Friday: 4 cups, no spill. Rani wants to find out the cause of the spilling, not just to avoid it for one day.
(a) On how many of the three 4-cup days did the dal spill?
(b) Does the data fully support the guess 'too much water makes it spill'? Why?
(c) Suggest one new guess she could test.
(d) Tomorrow she can cook with 3.5 cups, which never spilled, or with 4 cups and the one thing in her new guess changed. Which should she do, given her aim? Decide.
questions.a: (a) 2 of 3. (b) Only partly: Friday had 4 cups and no spill, so water alone does not explain every spill. (c) E.g. the flame was higher on the spill days. (d) 4 cups with the new guess changed (for example a lower flame): 3.5 cups would avoid a spill but test nothing, while changing one thing at 4 cups tests the new guess, which is what her aim of finding the cause needs.
s: Two of three days
Partly supported, with Friday as the exception
A new guess that can be tested
4 cups with one change, since only that tests the new guess and serves her aim

questions.q: Differentiate between 'a scientist' and 'someone working like a scientist' as the chapter uses them.
questions.a: Scientists are people who follow the scientific method to solve problems or discover new things; anyone who follows that method is working like a scientist, even in a kitchen or workshop.
s: Scientist: follows the method to solve problems or discover new things
Working like a scientist: anyone who follows the method

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter says learning science will develop our capabilities for finding solutions to bigger problems.
Reason (R): We all already apply the scientific method to some extent in daily life.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Mr Bhatt, a farmer, has never heard the words 'scientific method'. He noticed that the plants at one end of his field were wilting, wondered whether the water channel there was blocked, and walked along it to check. Which line of the chapter describes him best?
questions.a: We knowingly or unknowingly apply the method in daily life
o: We knowingly or unknowingly apply the method in daily life
Only people who know the method's name can be using it
Science is rarely done alone, so a farmer must first ask a whole team
The method's first step is to analyse the final results

questions.q: Write a new everyday situation, not from the chapter, in which a person follows the method: show the observation, question, guess and test.
questions.a: E.g. A vendor sees that the ice in her box melts quickly. Why? Maybe the box lid is loose. She closes it tightly the next day and watches; the ice lasts longer.
s: Observation
Question and guess
Test and result

questions.q:
An electrician logged 20 calls about lights that would not work: 12 were the bulb only, 6 were the switch only and 2 were both.
(i) What percentage of calls involved the bulb?
(ii) What percentage involved the switch?
(iii) On a new call, which guess should he test first, and why?
(iv) On a 'both' call, why would an electrician who stops as soon as he finds a bad bulb get the wrong answer?
(v) On a new call he fits a new bulb and the light comes on. Which step of the method is it when he then decides that the bulb was the fault?
questions.a: (i) (12 + 2)/20 = 70%. (ii) (6 + 2)/20 = 40%. (iii) The bulb, because it was involved in more calls (70% against 40%). (iv) After the new bulb is fitted the light still does not work, because the switch is also faulty; he must analyse whether the result really answers the question and test the switch too. (v) Analysing the results: he checks whether the result of his test answers his question.
s: Bulb first, with the 70% against 40% reason
On a 'both' call the light still fails after the bulb is changed, so he must check the result and test the switch
Analysis: deciding whether the test result answers the question

questions.q: Two electricians are called to a dark classroom. Ismail replaces the bulb, then the switch, without asking anything. Hema asks whether the fault is in the bulb or the switch and checks one at a time. Who is following the method the chapter describes?
questions.a: Hema, because she makes a guess and tests it
o: Hema, because she makes a guess and tests it
Ismail, because quickly replacing parts is the method
Both, because anyone who repairs a thing follows it
Neither, because only scientists in laboratories can

questions.q: Radha's mobile charger stops working. Name the observation and the question that start her investigation, in the chapter's steps.
questions.a: Observation: the charger does not charge her phone. Question: why is it not working?
s: Observation stated
Question stated

questions.q: True or False? Since everyone already applies the scientific method in daily life, learning science adds nothing more. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that though we all apply the scientific method to some extent, learning science will develop our capabilities for finding solutions to bigger problems and solving more mysteries of the universe.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: learning science develops our capabilities for bigger problems and more mysteries

questions.q:
Statement 1: A cook wondering whether too much water made the dal spill over is asking a question.
Statement 2: The chapter says learning science will help us find solutions to bigger problems.
Statement 3: Someone who swaps parts one after another without asking anything is following the method.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 1 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Salma's dal spills over. She asks whether there was too much water and uses less water the next day to see if it spills again. She says she is working like a scientist. Decide whether her claim is justified, using the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, it is justified. She observed the spill, asked a question, guessed (too much water) and tested by using less water. The chapter says anyone who follows the scientific method is working like a scientist, and its own example is a cook wondering why the dal spilled.
s: Verdict: yes, justified
Steps identified: observation, question, guess, test
Reason from the chapter: anyone following the method is working like a scientist

questions.q: Which person is NOT working like a scientist in the chapter's sense?
questions.a: A cook who throws away the spilled dal and never wonders why
o: A cook who throws away the spilled dal and never wonders why
A cook who wonders whether there was too much water in it
A bicycle repair person who asks where the air leaked out
An electrician who asks if the bulb or the switch is the problem

questions.q:
Neha's grandmother noticed a white layer on her pickle, wondered whether moisture had got into the jar, and kept the next batch in a dry jar with a tight lid to see if the layer came back.
(a) Name her guess and her test.
(b) Which of the chapter's examples, like her, guesses that too much of one thing (water or moisture) caused the problem? Explain the match.
questions.a: (a) Guess: moisture got into the jar. Test: keeping the next batch in a dry, tightly closed jar and watching. (b) The cook who wonders whether too much water made the dal spill out of the cooker; both suspect too much water and can test it by changing it the next time and watching.
s: Part (a): guess of moisture, tested with a dry tight jar
Part (b): the cook and the dal, both suspecting too much water

questions.q:
Two repair people get the same flat bicycle tyre. Arun pumps air into it; by evening it is flat again, so he pumps it again every morning for a week. Bina pumps it, wonders where the air is escaping, thinks 'maybe there is a hole in the tube', dips the tube in a tub of water a section at a time, sees bubbles near the valve, decides that is where the air escapes, and patches that spot.
(i) Which steps of the chapter's method does Bina carry out? Name each with what she did.
(ii) Which steps does Arun skip?
(iii) Arun says, 'My way also works: the tyre has air every morning.' Evaluate his claim.
(iv) Which of the two is working like a scientist in the chapter's sense, and why?
(v) If Bina had seen no bubbles, what should she have done next?
questions.a: (i) Observe: the tyre is flat; question: where does the air leak out?; guess: a hole in the tube; test: dipping the tube in water; analyse: bubbles near the valve show the leak. (ii) Arun only observes; he skips the question, the guess, the test and the analysis. (iii) It keeps the tyre usable for a day, but he never finds where the air leaks, so the cause stays unknown and the problem returns daily. (iv) Bina, because she follows the method, and the chapter says anyone who follows it is working like a scientist. (v) Make a new guess (for example that the valve itself leaks) and test it.
s: Bina's five steps named with what she did
Arun skips question, guess, test and analysis
Arun's claim judged: air every morning but the cause is never found
Bina is working like a scientist, because she follows the method
No bubbles: a new guess and a new test

questions.q: An electrician wants to know whether a classroom light failed because of the bulb or the switch. Show that replacing both at the same time cannot answer her question, and say what she should do instead.
questions.a: If both are replaced and the light works, either the old bulb or the old switch (or both) could have been faulty, so the result cannot tell her which. Only by testing one guess at a time, for example trying the bulb in a working holder first, can the result point to one cause.
s: If the light works after both are changed, either part could have been the fault
So the result cannot separate the two guesses
Instead test one at a time, such as the bulb in a working holder

questions.q:
The school gardener, Mr Ravi, notices that 12 of the 30 potted tomato plants on the terrace have yellow, drooping leaves, all at the sunny end. He wonders why only these 12 droop and guesses that they get too little water. For one week he gives each of the 12 an extra mug of water every evening and changes nothing else. At the end of the week, 8 of the 12 look healthy and 4 still droop. A teacher says, 'He is a gardener, not a scientist, so this is not science.'
(a) Write Mr Ravi's question and his guess as the chapter's method would put them, and say what his week of extra watering is in the method.
(b) Answer the teacher, using the chapter.
(c) What percentage of the 12 plants recovered? Does the result fully answer his question?
(d) Next week he can (P) give all 12 plants two extra mugs a day, or (Q) keep the one extra mug and look closely at the leaves and soil of the 4 drooping plants for insects. Which fits the chapter's method? Decide.
questions.a: (a) Question: why do only these 12 plants droop? Guess: they get too little water. The week of extra watering, with nothing else changed, is the test of that guess. (b) The chapter says anyone who follows the scientific method is working like a scientist; he observed, asked, guessed and tested, so he is working like one. (c) 8/12 = 66.7%. Only partly: 4 plants still droop, so too little water explains some of the plants but not all of them. (d) Q. The 4 plants did not recover with more water, so the water guess has already been tested on them and failed; a new guess (insects) must be made and tested by more observation. P only repeats the old guess and could overwater the 8 plants that are now healthy.
s: Question and guess stated; the extra watering is the test
Anyone who follows the method is working like a scientist
8/12 = 66.7%; only partly answered, since 4 still droop
Q: a new guess tested on the 4, P repeats a failed guess

questions.q: On a rainy afternoon, Class 6 is taken out to see the puddles in the school yard, and the children come back laughing and full of questions. Which line of the chapter does this match?
questions.a: Science is joyful exploration, like children enjoying the rain
o: Science is joyful exploration, like children enjoying the rain
Science is a list of facts learnt in class and then repeated
Science needs a laboratory and a full set of apparatus to begin
Science is complete once every question has been answered

questions.q:
Kavya and Rohan walk the same road to school every day. Kavya has noticed that the neem tree near the gate drops most of its leaves in one month of the year and wonders why; Rohan has never noticed the tree at all.
(a) Which two things that the chapter calls 'first and foremost' for learning science does Kavya show and Rohan lack?
(b) Write one how or why question Kavya could now pose about the tree.
questions.a: (a) Being curious and observing her surroundings keenly. (b) E.g. Why does the neem tree drop its leaves in one month and not spread through the year?
s: Part (a): curious and observing surroundings keenly
Part (b): a how or why question about the tree

questions.q: Riya tried 16 'why' questions on her own and was stuck on 9, so she asked her friends. Her brother says that is cheating, because real scientists always work by themselves. The chapter disagrees: it says science is rarely done ___.
questions.a: alone

questions.q: A teacher says, 'If you have not found answers to all your questions by the end of Grade 6, you have failed.' How does the chapter's closing section respond?
questions.a: Not all answers come in Grade 6; the journey runs five years or beyond
o: Not all answers come in Grade 6; the journey runs five years or beyond
It agrees, as Grade 6 is the only year of science the chapter discusses
Every question can be fully answered by the end of the first term
A student with open questions should stop wondering and memorise

questions.q: Gita tells her friends, 'I will start learning science properly once I get a microscope for my birthday. Until then I cannot.' Using the chapter's advice on learning science well, judge whether she is right.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that to learn science well, the first and foremost thing is to be curious and observe your surroundings keenly, and that when we are curious we start posing questions, asking how and why. None of this needs a microscope, so she can start now.
s: Verdict: no
First and foremost: be curious and observe surroundings keenly, then ask how and why
None of this needs equipment, so she can begin now

questions.q:
A Class 6 'Why? Club' logged 30 questions in a month. Every question was first tried by one member alone, and 9 were answered that way. Of the 21 left, 15 were taken to a group session, where 11 were answered and 4 stayed open. The other 6 have been tried alone only; they have not yet gone to a group session. The teacher has 3 extra periods for these 6 and can use them for more solo reading or for group sessions.
(a) Every question was tried alone before any group saw it. Which piece of the chapter's advice does this order follow?
(b) A member says the 10 questions still open show the club has failed. Which idea in the chapter's closing section answers him?
(c) What percentage of the questions tried alone were answered alone, and what percentage of those taken to a group were answered there?
(d) How should the 3 extra periods be used for the 6 questions? Decide, using the chapter's advice and the data.
questions.a: (a) 'If you cannot find an answer yourself, ask your friends to help you out': try first yourself, then go to others. (b) The world is full of things we do not know, things that are waiting to be explored; and you will not find answers to all your questions in Grade 6, so open questions are not failure. (c) Alone: 9/30 = 30%; in groups: 11/15 = 73.3%. (d) Group sessions: the 6 have already been tried alone without success, the chapter says to ask friends then because science is rarely done alone, and the club's own record shows groups answered 73.3% against 30% alone.
s: Try yourself first, then ask friends
The world is full of things waiting to be explored; not all answers come in Grade 6
Group sessions, since the 6 were already tried alone, the chapter says ask friends, and groups did better

questions.q: Sneha has tried for two days to find out why her class plant's leaves curl, and cannot find an answer. Which action matches the chapter's advice?
questions.a: Ask her friends to help, since discovering together is more fun
o: Ask her friends to help, since discovering together is more fun
Stop asking, since a Grade 6 student cannot find answers to such questions
Work alone for a whole year before asking anyone at all
Copy an answer from a book and treat the question as done

questions.q: Differentiate between learning science as 'joyful exploration' and learning it by memorising only.
questions.a: Joyful exploration means asking questions, observing and enjoying finding out, like children enjoying the rain. Memorising only means learning facts without wondering or asking.
s: Joyful exploration: questions, observing, enjoyment
Memorising only: facts without wondering

questions.q:
Statement 1: The chapter says scientists usually work alone and share their results with others only at the end.
Statement 2: The chapter says the journey of science ends with Grade 6.
Statement 3: The chapter's closing line ties being a wise person to asking 'why'.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 only
o: Statement 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only

questions.q: A student's science diary ends like this: '...so I still do not know why the Moon sometimes looks orange, but it is on my list for next year, and Priya and I will try again together.' Write two lines that could have come before this ending, and name two ideas from the chapter's closing section that the whole entry shows.
questions.a: E.g. 'Last night I saw an orange Moon low in the sky and wondered why. I looked for an answer on my own but could not find one, so I asked Priya.' Ideas: you will not find answers to all your questions in Grade 6, as the journey goes on for years; if you cannot find an answer yourself, ask your friends, since science is rarely done alone.
s: Two earlier lines: a noticed event and an attempt that did not find the answer
Idea 1: not all answers come in Grade 6; the journey continues
Idea 2: ask friends when you cannot find the answer yourself; science is rarely done alone

questions.q:
A school proposes four rules for its new Grade 6 science club.
Rule 1: Every member must find every answer alone; asking another member is not allowed.
Rule 2: A question not answered within one week must be crossed off and never asked again.
Rule 3: Each meeting starts with ten minutes of quietly observing something in the school garden and writing one how or why question about it.
Rule 4: Every member writes down a how or why question each week about something she noticed.
(i)-(iv) For each rule, say whether it agrees with the chapter, with the reason. (v) Rewrite Rule 1 so that it fits the chapter.
questions.a: (i) Rule 1 disagrees: science is rarely done alone, scientists work together in large teams, and the chapter says to ask friends when you cannot find an answer yourself. (ii) Rule 2 disagrees: not all answers will come in Grade 6, the journey runs five years or beyond, and the world is full of things waiting to be explored. (iii) Rule 3 agrees: the first and foremost thing is to be curious and observe your surroundings keenly, and curiosity leads to asking how and why. (iv) Rule 4 agrees: being curious leads us to pose questions, asking how and why, and to be a wise person you must be a 'whys' person. (v) 'Try to find the answer yourself first; if you cannot, ask your friends to help.'
s: Rule 1 disagrees: science is rarely done alone; ask friends
Rule 2 disagrees: answers need not all come in Grade 6; things wait to be explored
Rule 3 agrees: be curious and observe keenly, then ask how and why
Rule 4 agrees: a wise person is a 'whys' person
Rule 1 rewritten: try yourself first, then ask friends

questions.q: Veer stops asking 'why' whenever he cannot solve a question. Mitra writes her unanswered questions in a list to come back to later. Whose approach is closer to the chapter?
questions.a: Mitra's, because the world is full of things waiting to be explored
o: Mitra's, because the world is full of things waiting to be explored
Veer's, because an unanswered question shows that a student should stop
Both are equal, because the chapter never mentions open questions
Veer's, because the chapter says to avoid hard questions in Grade 6

questions.q: True or False? When the chapter says the world is full of things we do not know, it means students should feel worried about how little they know. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says these are things that are waiting to be explored, calls science joyful exploration, and asks us never to stop wondering; not knowing is an invitation, not a worry.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the unknown things are waiting to be explored, in a joyful journey

questions.q: A notice on a classroom wall reads: 'Working with friends on a science question is cheating.' Reply to it using the chapter, in two points.
questions.a: The chapter says science is rarely done alone and that scientists across the world work together, often in large teams. It also says it is always more fun to discover things together.
s: Science is rarely done alone; scientists work in teams
More fun to discover together

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter advises a student who cannot find an answer alone to ask friends.
Reason (R): Science is rarely done alone; scientists across the world work together, often in large teams.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Show that a Grade 6 student cannot expect to answer every question she asks by the end of Grade 6, using two ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: Every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions, so each answer she finds adds new questions to her list instead of shortening it. There is also no limit to what we can discover, and the world is full of things we do not know. So her list can never be emptied, and some questions must still be open at the end of Grade 6.
s: First idea: every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions
Second idea: there is no limit to what can be discovered
Conclusion: answering adds questions, so the list never empties and some remain

questions.q:
For two weeks, two Class 6 groups kept a 'Wonder Diary'. Group P wrote down only what they saw, such as 'ants on the wall' or 'clouds at noon': 40 entries and 2 questions. Group Q wrote what they saw and then asked how or why about it: 22 entries and 18 questions. Of Q's questions, 7 were answered by trying themselves, 6 after asking another group, and 5 remain open. Only one diary can be shown at the school's open day.
(a) Which of the chapter's 'first and foremost' needs does Group P show, and what does it leave out that Group Q shows?
(b) Of Group Q's questions, 6 were answered only after asking another group and 5 remain open. Which idea in the chapter does each of these two facts support?
(c) Which diary should be shown to illustrate the chapter's idea of learning science? Decide, using (a) and (b) and the numbers.
questions.a: (a) Group P observes keenly (40 entries) but leaves out curiosity: posing questions, asking how and why, which Group Q does. (b) The 6 support 'science is rarely done alone, so if you cannot find an answer yourself, ask your friends'; the 5 open ones support 'you will not find answers to all your questions in Grade 6' and that the world is full of things waiting to be explored. (c) Group Q's diary: P has more entries (40 against 22), but Q shows both halves of the 'first and foremost' advice, turns its observations into 18 questions against P's 2, answers 6 of 18 (a third) with others' help, and keeps 5 open for later.
s: P observes keenly but does not pose how or why questions as Q does
The 6: science is rarely done alone; the 5: not all answers come in Grade 6
Group Q's diary, weighing P's 40 entries against Q's 18 questions and team work

questions.q: A classmate says the chapter's closing line, 'to be a wise person, you must be a "whys" person', is just a joke on two words that sound alike. (a) What does the line ask a student to do? (b) Show that it fits the rest of the chapter's advice.
questions.a: (a) To keep asking 'why' about what she sees. (b) The chapter says that when we are curious we start posing questions, asking how and why, and calls curiosity the first and foremost thing for learning science; the line packs that advice into a memorable pun.
s: Part (a): keep asking why
Part (b): matches the advice that curiosity leads to asking how and why

questions.q: Which statement is NOT made in the chapter's closing sections?
questions.a: Science should be done seriously and quietly, never for fun
o: Science should be done seriously and quietly, never for fun
It is always more fun to discover things together
Never stop wondering about the amazing mysteries of the universe
To be a wise person, you must be a 'whys' person

questions.q: The chapter's Activity 1.3 asks: if you had to ask 'Why?' about something, what would you ask about, and how would you try to find an answer? Do this for one thing in your home or street. Write it in five parts: what you noticed; your why question; how you would try to find the answer yourself; whom you would turn to if you could not; and what you would do if the answer still had not come by the end of Grade 6.
questions.a: E.g. (1) The steel tumbler on our table has drops of water on the outside on hot days but not on cold days. (2) Why do drops appear on the outside only on hot days? (3) I would watch it on several hot and cold days, with cold and warm water inside, and note when drops form. (4) If I could not work it out, I would ask my friends to try it with me, since science is rarely done alone. (5) I would keep it on my list, because not every answer comes in Grade 6 and the journey goes on for years.
s: A real observation from home or street
A why question that grows from that observation
A way to try to find the answer by observing or testing
Turning to friends when stuck, linked to science being rarely done alone
Keeping the question for later, linked to the journey beyond Grade 6
